Yes. 

The manipulation of time in the story is very effective and well-balanced, matching the retrospective and introspective tone of the narrator. 

**Compression of time** is used masterfully to cover an entire academic year—from October to May—and eventually a jump of several years into the narrator's present life as a teacher. Rather than bogging the narrative down in day-to-day minutiae, the author summarizes months of relationship building, habits, and atmosphere in single sentences or paragraphs (e.g., "Within a month, a version of me circulated...", "In February, when the river froze..."). This establishes the routine and the slow accumulation of the "versions" of the narrator created by others.

**Stretching of time** (or slowing the pace down to real-time scenes) is used selectively for moments of emotional rupture and truth. The narrative slows down to focus on specific, brief moments: Lizzy's confession over cold coffee in March, Martin folding shirts in the laundromat, and the pivotal moment in April when Johan speaks in class. In the classroom scene, time stretches as the narrator processes the silence, the clicking radiator, her idle pen, and the profound internal realization that Johan is reading her rather than the poem. 

By compressing the months of self-deception and "management" and stretching the brief, sharp moments of honesty, the pacing directly reinforces the central theme of the story.
